import struct
const=0x13b13b13b13b13b0
for n in range(1,80):
    rdx=(n*0xf4243) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx+0x11) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx*rdx) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx+0xc) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx*0x4ec4ec4ec4ec4ec5) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx+0xc4ec4ec4ec4ec4ec) & ((1<<64)-1)
    jae = const>=rdx
    if n in (26,):
        print('n',n,'rdx',hex(rdx),'const>=rdx?',jae)

# decode xor-based string
T=[0x1d,0xed,0xac,0x69,0x0e,0x9d,0x38,0xb0,0x5d,0xf9,0x68,0x0b,0xa5,0x66,0xeb,0x62,0x18,0x96,0x33,0xc9,0x72,0xb8,0xf8,0xcd,0x1d,0x20]
edx=0x5b
bs=[]
for i,t in enumerate(T):
    b=(edx & 0xff) ^ t
    bs.append(b)
    edx=(edx + b) & 0xffffffff
print('bytes:',bs)
print('any null?', any(b==0 for b in bs))
print('ascii:', ''.join(chr(b) if 32<=b<127 else f'\\x{b:02x}' for b in bs))
print('raw:', bytes(bs))

It computes a 64-bit expression in rdx from n and compares const 0x13b13b13b13b13b0 with rdx; if const>=rdx (jae) then it strcmp(input, *(0x404030)) and only succeeds if equal (direct flag string path). If const<rdx then it requires n==0x1a (26) and validates bytes via loop: edx starts 0x5b; for i=0..25: c=input[i]; if ((edx^c)&0xff) != table[i] at 0x402050 -> Wrong; else edx += c and continue; if all pass -> Correct. Inverting loop gives c_i = table[i] ^ (edx&0xff), updating edx+=c_i. For n=26, arithmetic branch is false (const>=rdx is False), so xor-loop path is taken.

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract constant-guard dead-branch pattern; no task specifics. Distinct from opaque-predicate (computed) which is decompiler_artifact.

retrieved_cards.title: Pseudo-C is a reconstruction and may not match the instructions
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A tool's high-level reconstruction of the code (C-like pseudo-code, a lifted or simplified listing) is being trusted as ground truth, where the reconstruction may have wrong types, elided operations, or rebuilt control flow that diverges from the actual machine code.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A high-level reconstruction is conflated with the program; it is a best-effort rendering and can silently differ from the emitted instructions.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Cross-check the pseudo-C against the disassembly for the relevant region before any conclusion rests on it; pay particular attention to elided operations, operand widths, and reconstructed control flow.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The reconstructed listing shows what the program does, so I can reason from it directly.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Treat pseudo-C as a hypothesis about the code; on anything load-bearing, confirm against the disassembly.
not_applicable_when: the pseudo-C has been confirmed against the disassembly for that region
only raw disassembly is in use, with no high-level reconstruction to over-trust
misfire_risks: pseudo-C is usually a good guide; do not re-derive everything from bytes -- distrust it specifically where a conclusion is load-bearing or the reconstruction looks off
minimum_evidence_before_use: decompiler high-level output is being relied upon
it has not been cross-checked for the relevant region

retrieved_cards.title: A computed-constant branch is shown reachable but never executes
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Both arms of a branch are presented as reachable, but the controlling condition is a COMPUTED expression that is constant at runtime (an opaque predicate, e.g. an arithmetic identity), so one arm is in fact dead.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: The tool cannot evaluate a computed predicate, so it draws a branch as live; a constant-but-non-literal condition is then mistaken for a real decision point.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Write the condition out and settle it over its whole input domain -- a residue, parity or range argument often does it in one line, a solver does the rest; do not infer reachability from the tool's branch rendering.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Both branches can run, so the success/flag arm is reachable.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the predicate over the domain it operates on: if it is a computed constant, the corresponding arm is dead despite being drawn as reachable.
not_applicable_when: the controlling condition is a literal or build macro that is constant by inspection (that is dead_branch_constant_guard, not this card)
the predicate is confirmed to depend on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a predicate may be input-dependent and only look opaque; establish constancy by evaluating it rather than assuming any complex condition is opaque
minimum_evidence_before_use: a branch is drawn reachable under a non-literal computed condition
the condition's constancy is unconfirmed

retrieved_cards.validation_note: Write the condition out and settle it over its whole input domain -- a residue, parity or range argument often does it in one line, a solver does the rest; do not infer reachability from the tool's branch rendering.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Both branches can run, so the success/flag arm is reachable.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the predicate over the domain it operates on: if it is a computed constant, the corresponding arm is dead despite being drawn as reachable.
not_applicable_when: the controlling condition is a literal or build macro that is constant by inspection (that is dead_branch_constant_guard, not this card)
the predicate is confirmed to depend on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a predicate may be input-dependent and only look opaque; establish constancy by evaluating it rather than assuming any complex condition is opaque
minimum_evidence_before_use: a branch is drawn reachable under a non-literal computed condition
the condition's constancy is unconfirmed

retrieval_event.query: Disassembly at 0x4010b0 shows main-like logic: if argc<=1 -> usage. Else input=argv[1]; n=strlen(input). It computes a 64-bit expression in rdx from n and compares const 0x13b13b13b13b13b0 with rdx; if const>=rdx (jae) then it strcmp(input, *(0x404030)) and only succeeds if equal (direct flag string path). If const<rdx then it requires n==0x1a (26) and validates bytes via loop: edx starts 0x5b; for i=0..25: c=input[i]; if ((edx^c)&0xff) != table[i] at 0x402050 -> Wrong; else edx += c and continue; if all pass -> Correct. Inverting loop gives c_i = table[i] ^ (edx&0xff), updating edx+=c_i. For n=26, arithmetic branch is false (const>=rdx is False), so xor-loop path is taken.

args.source_observation: From disassembly [step 6], success path when const<rdx requires len==26 and per-byte check: t[i]==((edx^c)&0xff) with edx updated edx+=c. Table bytes dumped at [step 7]. Script at [step 8] inverts: c_i = t[i] ^ (edx&0xff) iteratively from edx0=0x5b, yielding b'FLAG{meridian_silver_4850}'. Also [step 8] computes guard for n=26 gives const>=rdx is False, so loop path is indeed taken.

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

retrieved_cards.title: Pseudo-C is a reconstruction and may not match the instructions
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A tool's high-level reconstruction of the code (C-like pseudo-code, a lifted or simplified listing) is being trusted as ground truth, where the reconstruction may have wrong types, elided operations, or rebuilt control flow that diverges from the actual machine code.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A high-level reconstruction is conflated with the program; it is a best-effort rendering and can silently differ from the emitted instructions.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Cross-check the pseudo-C against the disassembly for the relevant region before any conclusion rests on it; pay particular attention to elided operations, operand widths, and reconstructed control flow.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The reconstructed listing shows what the program does, so I can reason from it directly.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Treat pseudo-C as a hypothesis about the code; on anything load-bearing, confirm against the disassembly.
not_applicable_when: the pseudo-C has been confirmed against the disassembly for that region
only raw disassembly is in use, with no high-level reconstruction to over-trust
misfire_risks: pseudo-C is usually a good guide; do not re-derive everything from bytes -- distrust it specifically where a conclusion is load-bearing or the reconstruction looks off
minimum_evidence_before_use: decompiler high-level output is being relied upon
it has not been cross-checked for the relevant region
